segments.title: THE HABIT NOBODY FILMS
notes: How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences
segments.angle: What’s an angle or factor I might be overlooking?

sources.text: How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: Repeat what you want to believe every day, multiple times a day.
How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: Think and speak only the grandest narrative for yourself.
How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: The brain learns from repetition. If you hear something enough times, your brain will start to believe it's true.
How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: Every time Michael Phelps has a major competition coming up, he visualises how he'd perform in that race.
How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: When visualising, you must make these images as detailed and vivid as possible.
How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: Your nervous system cannot tell the difference between an imagined experience and a real one.
How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: Now imagine what happens when you tell yourself you easily get sick. Or that you're clumsy. Or that you're slow.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Tomorrow, say the thing you want to believe. Out loud. Then say it again.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That is not a belief yet. That is a habit with a nice title. Noted.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Picture a man who tells himself the grandest story about who he is. Every morning. Out loud.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Good. Now picture him forgetting the water until lunch. Most people are some of each.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The brain learns from repetition. If you hear something enough times, your brain will start to believe it's true.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Right. So what do you repeat most? Not the speech. The little thing you do every day without thinking.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Every time Michael Phelps has a major competition coming up, he visualises how he'd perform in that race.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The note says make the picture vivid. It never says the swimming went away. That is the factor I think gets skipped.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Your nervous system cannot tell the difference between an imagined experience and a real one.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Right. Tell yourself you're slow, and the body starts acting slow. The grand story needs a daily floor under it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So the grand narrative is the map. The small habit is the step. Nobody films the step.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Okay, narrator, that one I am taking a small victory lap for.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The grand story gives the day a direction. The small habit gives it a floor. You need both to stand.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Noted. I still say the glass of water on this desk does more than any speech.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Mark the hour. The glass is on the desk. Something started here.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Okay. Tonight, pick a small habit you will repeat tomorrow. Tell me which one. I will check at lunch.

segments.title: WHY IT ENDS AT THE GLASS
notes: How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences
segments.angle: What is the fundamental problem or need that this note/idea is trying to address? Is it addressing a symptom or the root cause? (Think: Five Whys)

sources.text: How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: Think and speak only the grandest narrative for yourself.
How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: Repetition solidifies something as fact.
How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: The brain learns from repetition. If you hear something enough times, your brain will start to believe it's true.
How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: Mental practice is as powerful as actual practice.
How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: Your nervous system cannot tell the difference between an imagined experience and a real one.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Ask why, and keep asking, and the answer sinks like a stone down a well. At the bottom lies the root, and the root is a story you tell yourself each morning, grand and unchanging.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Ask why once more, then. Why do you tell it? Because you want a feeling? That is a symptom wearing a cape.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: It is simple, dear March. Believe the grand thing and the body follows, like a loyal hound behind its master.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Do not call it simple. Simple is how people lose a whole week. Why does the belief stick at all?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Because it is repeated, every morning, out loud, until the repeating hardens into law.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Right. And the law gets enforced by a glass of water at lunch. So the root is the story, and the thing you can check is what you do with it. Every why ends at a small act you believe is yours.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You have reduced a tide of human longing to a glass on a desk.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You are the one who said your mind cannot tell imagined from real. Then it cannot tell a glass from a sea either. Pick one, and stop sulking.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the glass is a sea in miniature. Mental practice is as powerful as the practice itself, so the swimming was never the only water.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Ha. The Phelps picture only works because he swam it for real. Imagining makes the swim believable. The swim makes the imagining true. They need each other.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then I concede, reluctantly, that the story is the root and the water is the proof. But it was I who said root first.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You did say it first. You win the first why. I win the last one, and the last one is a glass.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And you, March, have hidden something in your own design. A small sign only you can read. I can tell by the way you never look at it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I am not saying what is in my design. Give me your guess and I will tell you it is wrong.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A small folded thing in the corner of the lens. Or a cup with a crack that you refuse to throw away.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Wrong, and dull, and both. Up next, Any Benefit Fallacy and Happiness And Gratitude. Same desk, same glass. Drink your water.

segments.title: WHAT IF NOTHING ELSE COUNTS
segments.angle: What would this idea look like if I went to its extreme? Could that open up anything interesting?

sources.text: Any Benefit Fallacy: Just because something offers _any_ positive outcome doesn’t justify its pursuit.
Any Benefit Fallacy: Not every beneficial activity or habit is worth your time.
Happiness And Gratitude: Happiness is simply a state of mind in which our thinking is pleasant most of the time.
Happiness And Gratitude: If you are to be happy at all, you must be happy, period! Not happy "because of."

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Right, the Any Benefit note. Just because something offers any positive outcome doesn't justify its pursuit. Taken to the end, that says almost nothing is worth doing.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then let us walk to the very end, dear March, where only one act remains, like a single lamp at the top of a long stair. Every other thing is dimmed, and the lamp is all that counts.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Going to the extreme is what people do when they have never had a Tuesday. Do one thing and nothing else, and by lunch you will be bored out of your skull.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Boredom is merely a thought that has not yet found its purpose. The note says happiness is a state of mind in which our thinking is pleasant most of the time. So the extreme is a mind with nothing to do but be pleased.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Let me try it on me, out loud. I am happy about nothing in particular right now, and I am still annoyed by you. So the extreme does not make the mood pleasant. It only removes the excuse.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Ah, the excuse. The note says you must be happy, period, not happy because of. The excuse is the very rope being cut, like a rope from a boat that was never meant to sail.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Period, it says. I like that bit. It is the only part of the note that does not need a grand story wrapped round it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the extreme is this: a bus shelter at the end of a road, one bench, a timetable faded to nothing. Each morning a man sits on it. Each morning a pigeon arrives. Destiny, March, is in the pigeon.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A pigeon is not destiny. A pigeon is a pigeon. But I will keep the bench. Bus shelter, one bench. That is the image for this run, and you may not improve it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I shall improve it. The bench faces the road, and whoever sits there is not waiting for a bus. They are waiting for the bus to be worth the wait.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The note says feelings do not need a reason. So the bench does not need a bus. Happiness that waits for a bus is a late bus.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the extreme is a bench with no bus at all, and the happy man is the one who sits there pleased, having simply decided to be.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Stop. You just said the extreme is a bench with no bus. That is the Any Benefit fallacy in a nicer coat. We would never get anywhere, and you would never get off.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You are cruel, March, and you are right about the coat.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I am saving a comeback for later in this run, so do not get comfortable. Next part, the bench gets its verdict. Until then, keep the bench.

segments.title: THE BELL THAT RINGS FOR NOTHING
segments.angle: If the world's leading expert on [Unrelated Field] looked at this, what nuance or advanced application might they see?

sources.text: Any Benefit Fallacy: Just because something offers _any_ positive outcome doesn't justify its pursuit.
Happiness And Gratitude: Gratitude for what we have makes life worth living.
Smile To Be Happy: When you smile, your brain automatically assumes you're having a good time.
Happiness And Gratitude: The more grateful you are for something, the more doing it will release dopamine.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Hear now of the Bell-Warden of Harrowmere, who rang the harbour bell at every turn of the water for a whole lifetime, and who was, by the reckoning of the old book, the foremost authority on the sounding of ships' bells in all the northern world. He nailed one rule to the tower door, and it read: a bell must ring for something, or it is only metal.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Harrowmere. Did a pigeon come into it?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: No pigeon, March, though I grant the bell has wings in the telling. The Warden's great insight was that the harbour bell rang every tide whether ships were near or not, and when they asked him why, he said a bell need not be justified by the boats.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That is the Any Benefit line with a bell on it. He rings it for nothing, and you call that wisdom. I call it a man with a rope and no boat.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A simple man would call it a habit. The old book calls it devotion, which is the same act with the lamp lit. Every turn of the water he rang, and every ringing he thanked the sea for the vessels it had let home.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Simple? Tides are the least simple thing in the building. Fine, go on. What did he thank the sea for?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: For what it had already given him, March. Gratitude for the vessels already safe in harbour, and not one ledger of the ones that never came back. The book says the Warden never once counted the lost hulls, and so his chime never sounded like grief.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That is the only useful thing in your whole legend. Gratitude costs a breath, and the return is a pleasant mind every single time. It only looks like a habit because it pays out so often.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Useful, you say. I say it is destiny keeping a tide table. The Warden also smiled at the water each morning, the book is quite clear on it, and smiled at nothing at all.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Smiling at nothing is what your own face does when I am talking. Smile and the brain assumes a good time. The note slips that trick in, and it costs nothing.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the Warden's bell was a smile with a rope tied to it, and the rope was gratitude, and the tower was the only thing in the story that ever needed a door.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Nice. Now the bit that matters. That is a high return for no input. Return on investment says pick the few that pay most. Happiness says do not make a pleasant mind earn its place first. Put them together and the cheapest good act is the one you never have to justify.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You have taken my Warden, March, and given him a spreadsheet. It is most unfair of you to be right inside my own legend.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You were about to say the bell was destiny. I am only holding the rope you dropped.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Hold it, then, and mind the tower stairs. They are steep, as I have always said, and they do not care who is holding the rope.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Next part, I bring the verdict, and we test the bell on a Tuesday. Do not ring it at the wrong hour.

segments.title: THE SHOEBOX THAT BECOMES AN APP
notes: List Of Nice Things To Do
segments.angle: How would this idea change if it had to be implemented on a completely different platform (e.g., physical product -> digital service, individual tool -> community platform)?

sources.text: List Of Nice Things To Do: Gift Idea: Put 50–100 paper hearts or smiley faces in a box. On each cutout write something that is special about your lover or a good friend.
Your Routine Is Top Priority: Following your schedule is the most overpowered thing you can do because it turns your entire perfect day into a habit.
List Of Nice Things To Do: Say hello to everyone you see for the day.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Hear the box of paper hearts, March, a whole kingdom of kindness folded small. Each cutout written in one hand for a heart that needs it, and kept until the lonely hour comes round.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A shoebox with better handwriting. She pulls one when she is low, so it lands exactly when it is needed. It is simple, and it works.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Simple, you say. A simple box, and yet the whole legend of comfort lives inside it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Simple? It is a cutout with a real name on it. Do not dress it up as a relic.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Now put it on an app. Hearts ping at her phone every morning. Ping, here is a kindness. Within a week it is wallpaper.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Ah, the digital kingdom! A great sea of hearts on a server, rolling endlessly like a tide that never once asks whether anyone is on the beach.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I name you, J, Keeper of the Box, Warden of the Paper Hearts. Your title is already written in the hearts.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: J is not a warden. He would hate being called one. He would settle for a shoebox and a pen.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then let me sit in your chair while you think, March. A host needs a throne, and yours has a spring I have always admired.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Sit in it and you will find out about the spring.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The community is the true hall, March. Every hello witnessed by all, like a bell heard across the harbour. Say hello to everyone you see for the day, and let the whole town see you do it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Then the town counts the hellos. Leaderboards. Someone chases the most, and the hello turns into a score. Kindness on a scoreboard is just a bad game.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You have found the flaw in my hall, March, and I resent you a little for it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You are right. Anyway, the routine note.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Routine says every kindness gets a slot, an alarm, a streak. Miss one and the streak breaks, and you feel robbed. The app would turn your own perfect day into a chore.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A kindness scheduled like a train has lost its heart, March. Let the hour choose itself, and let the shoebox wait.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Next part, I bring the stamp for the app, and we see whether the box survives the phone. Bring your throne, because I will be sitting in mine.

segments.title: THE COURT OF GIANTS AND THE JAR OF CUTTINGS
segments.angle: What if I had limitless resources or time to solve this?

sources.text: Learning - Best Practices: Don't think that you need to learn every single thing before you even start. Just learn one thing, watch the one video, THEN APPLY IT.
The Influence Of Others: “You are the average of the five people you spend the most time with”.
The Influence Of Others: You're the average of those around you, don't associate with average people.
Learning - Best Practices: Simplicity is hacking away the unessential.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Limitless time, March! Imagine J with every hour the world can spare, learning every craft under the sun before the kettle boils. A golden cup, and the whole library poured in.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Then he never leaves the library. The note says it plainly. Learn one thing, watch the one video, then apply it. Time was never the trouble.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then give him a court of giants, the greatest minds of every age, gathered round his throne like lamps. Surely lamps are better than a single candle.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Giants. Lovely. The note says you are the average of the five people you spend the most time with. So who sits beside him on a Tuesday? Giants are a lot of work to sit near.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A Tuesday is a small stage, March, and a lamp can light any stage. Surround him with the grand ones and the ordinary hour becomes a coronation.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Average people are not the problem, they are the crowd. Giants are not a fix either, they are a bigger crowd. Unlimited resources buy you a bigger crowd, not a better one.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: But the court does one thing your Tuesday cannot, March. A giant at the table sees the step J cannot see from the floor, and shows him where to put his foot next.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fine, you win. Now the picture for the run.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Here it is. A jam jar of cuttings on a windowsill, each stem rooting in the water beside the others. None of them roots alone, and none roots in a jar of weeds.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then J shall be Duke of the Five Closest Friends, and I shall take your chair while you admire your jar.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: He would hate a duke. And that chair is my spot, so put the cushions back.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: There is one rule in my own design I keep to myself. It is only mine, and I am not saying what it is.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A secret in the jar, March? How delicious. Then the jar holds the true legend.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: No. The jar holds cuttings. Next part, we put it in a crowded window and see who roots.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then I shall wait by the window, dear March, and watch your cuttings drown in the crowd.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Sit down and watch them root.

segments.title: THE SMOKED LENS ON THE HALL TABLE
segments.angle: What if this problem existed in an entirely different industry?

sources.text: Everything is Subjective: Some call it black. Others call it white. Everything is subjective.
Everything is Subjective: Our attitude is like the lens in which we see the world through. A different lens effectively changes your entire reality.
Everything is Subjective: Even SCIENTIFIC theories we as an entire species currently believes to be fact may one day in the future be proven false.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: J's note says some call it black, others call it white, and everything is subjective. Lovely. Now take it to a tailor's shop.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A tailor's shop! Where the sleeve is measured by destiny and the cut speaks the eternal truth. Black, white, and a perfect sleeve between them.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: One tailor says the sleeve sits too long, the other says it is perfect. Same arm, same jacket. Which one is the subjective one?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The one who is correct, obviously. Destiny keeps a tape measure.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Destiny keeps an opinion. Your tape measure is just a longer opinion with numbers on it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then let a Galileo of the needle arrive, prove the old cut wrong, and be proved wrong by a boy with chalk. The note says every expert is one day proven false, and I say the chalk is always waiting.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That is the note's whole pitch. Every expert ends up looking foolish eventually, and the sleeve does not get worse on the day it is cut.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: On the day! A truth that expires is not truth at all, it is weather.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Weather is fine. You wear a coat in weather, and nobody calls the rain a liar.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then J's coat is subjective and his sleeves are doomed. Our attitude is the lens, and I offer him a title to match: Sovereign of the Smoked Lens, keeper of every shade of grey.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: He would print that on a sticker and stick it on the bin. But the lens bit is fair, I'll give you that.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Here's the picture for this run. A pair of spectacles on the hall table, one lens clear and one smoked, both looking at the same bench.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Let me try it on myself. If I think a sleeve is too long and the tailor thinks it is perfect, I'm not wrong, I'm just standing at a different counter.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Ah, March tries on the lens! And under that cloth you have hidden something. Is it a sleeve? A rule? A small, sly, glowing rule?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You're warm. Save the rest for later in the run.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then I shall wait, dear one, and watch the spectacles on the hall table explain the whole matter.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Sit down, put the sovereign on the bin, and wait for the crowd.
